speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: Hey, this is Carlos, CEO at Product School and your host on The Product Podcast. My guest today is Maggie Crowley, VP of Product at Toast. Two fun facts before we start: she finished fifth at the 2006 Winter Olympics as a speed skater, and she was contributing to Product School years ago, back when she was at Drift. Toast is the point of sale behind the restaurants and coffee shops you already pay at, and her customers are not on X all day. They are running slim-margin businesses that have zero patience for AI theater. Things we'll cover in this episode: shipping AI into a 14-year-old platform, not a blank slate; ten customers, one WhatsApp group, a year of iterating before GA; the least tech-savvy operators loved it first, and why; how long you have before consumer patterns become your users' expectations; and a live demo changing a real menu price from chat. Let's get into it. Welcome to The Product Podcast, Maggie. Thank you so much.

speaker: Maggie Crowley
text: Happy to be here. Two Fun Facts: The Olympics and Drift

speaker: Maggie Crowley

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia

speaker: Maggie Crowley
text: Yes, yes. It feels like not as long ago as it actually was, unfortunately.

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia

speaker: Maggie Crowley
text: Absolutely. Toast is a retail and restaurant point of sale. It's the thing where, if you go to a restaurant or a coffee shop and you want to pay for a meal, you're probably swiping your card, whether it's at a kiosk, at a counter, or maybe there's a handheld they bring around where you swipe your card. That's the thing most people interact with. But behind the scenes, it's the hardware in the store itself, and all of the software that helps our operators run their menus, their inventory, their team schedule, their prep, and how they understand how their business is doing. So there's a whole host of things happening above store. We also have a bunch of products for how we help our operators drive traffic to their locations. And then we have a consumer app as well. Building for People Who Aren't on X

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: Those are the things I want to unpack. We spend a lot of time on X, and we're hopefully at the forefront of AI in some ways. But ultimately, I think you're building a product for a lot of people who are not on X, right? That's the real economy. So the way you build for them and drive adoption is different than some of the keynotes we see from OpenAI or Anthropic.

speaker: Maggie Crowley
text: That's true. I always think about our role at Toast as: these operators are super sophisticated, they run really difficult, slim-margin businesses, and they do it largely because they love it. Our job is to figure out how we take all that technology coming out of Anthropic or OpenAI or whoever, and put it to work for them, so they don't have to spend time thinking about which model to use or how to set up a workflow. Our job is to figure out how we make it useful for them, and then how we make it something that is actually real and not a distraction. There's so much you could do with AI, and there's so much theater around feeling like you've done something. But the question is, did it actually drive an outcome? Did it help you make more money? Did it help you save money? Did it save you real time? That's the bar I think about when we're building with these tools for businesses, and it's a different type of challenge that I find really interesting. Shipping AI Into a Platform That Existed Before AI

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: One thing I noticed you mentioned on X recently is that you're building agents within SaaS products that existed before AI. That's a key difference from AI-native products that didn't have something to compare with. So from your perspective, what does that really mean, and how is it different from a native product?

speaker: Maggie Crowley
text: There are a couple of challenges. One is that your customers, if you're lucky, already know what they use you for. They have really specific ways they've set up their workflows, whether that's just the muscle memory of how they use your tool, or specific workflows in the tool. They're used to doing that. So anything you want to do has to convince them to do it in a different way. There's a layer of behavior change you have to figure out. There's also the question of how much change your customers can absorb. Do they want to try something new? Is the thing your AI tool does actually germane to the outcome they're trying to get, and how do you make it useful for them? How do you make them want to use it? And then there's a scale question, which is that you can't necessarily launch something that doesn't work, isn't fast, isn't accurate, or isn't performant to your install base. Because then they're going to not want to use your product, and you're going to burn trust. If you're early, there's a bit of a sense that you can just try things and test them out. There are lots of things we're seeing come through a channel like X that are early, a little bit broken, maybe the integrations aren't great or the security isn't perfect, but that's okay, because we're all early adopters. When you're building AI in a platform like Toast, you have to think about the bar for quality and excellence being really high from the start. So you have to get creative about how you build in that environment. It's not that you can't build quickly and iteratively; it's just a different way of thinking about it. The Design-Partner Playbook

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: So how are you building in that environment?

speaker: Maggie Crowley
text: The way we thought about it, in the very early days when we started working on this at the end of 2023, we didn't even really know exactly what the use case would end up being. But we knew this technology was coming, and we wanted to start trying. So we found just a handful of design partners, as we called them, and we put ourselves in WhatsApp groups with these customers. We started turning an assistant on. We picked one platform, so we started on mobile just to make it easy for ourselves, and we picked one use case around reporting. We shipped it to these ten people, and we walled ourselves off to iterate with them as fast as we could, to get to a point where the product was good enough that we could start to scale it. We've done that with every major feature we've released since then. We did that for honestly about a year. Then the models finally got good enough in early 2025, and we made it generally available last fall, in October, and have built a lot into it since. But it was really that process: finding a couple of customers, building really quickly and iteratively with them, being in a channel where you could get fast feedback, and then scaling from there. That's how we figured out how to operate. Probably the other thing that's unique about building in this space is that you have to bring the AI to your customer. We couldn't assume they'd discover it on their own. Just adding a chat box somewhere isn't enough. You have to bring it to them. You have to get them over the blank-page problem. You have to help them understand when to use it. And an enduring challenge of these tools is that even if you get one of your users to use it, you're probably adding all sorts of capabilities in the background, and there's no way for them to see that, because it's all behind the scenes. So you have to constantly think about how you get them to use it, and then how you help them understand everything you're adding. You have to constantly re-onboard your users, because it's constantly changing. It's an interesting way to think about a product. Maybe before, you could launch something and assume that once your user figured it out and used it once, they understood how it worked. That's not the case with AI. You have to build a better muscle around bringing the product to them, helping them understand what it does, and then re-engaging them when you have new things. Re-Onboarding Users Who Have Other Jobs to Do

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: I think that's a good point. Onboarding has always been critical, but especially as you start shipping more stuff. How do you do that, especially for someone who is probably doing other things? We go to bed thinking about the product we're building, but they probably have other things to figure out. So how do you do that type of onboarding differently now, to make sure it's driving the right level of adoption for those new capabilities?

speaker: Maggie Crowley
text: If I had totally cracked the onboarding problem for an AI product, maybe I'd have my own startup, I don't know. The way we think about it: the more you understand your customer, your user, the way they're working, and what they're up to, the better you're going to be at figuring out when they should use the thing you're building. And that's the same as any product you'd build. But you have to really understand, for us physically, where they are in the store or the restaurant. What time of day is it? Is it during a shift or not? What role do they have in the restaurant or retail shop, and where are they? And then, what might they need to do? And how do you close that gap and bring them whatever the use case is at that moment? So practically speaking, we of course have this assistant, Toast IQ, in our product. But it's entry points throughout the product. It's pre-written prompts that we know work really well, that we know are questions they're going to ask. And it's making sure it works really well in our mobile app as well as our desktop, and that we tailor the starter prompts based on what they're doing on those platforms at different times of day. So it's about getting really specific about all of those things and trying to make it really easy for them to get started. Once they get in and start asking their questions, then it's relatively easy; you just have to figure out how to get them in to start. From "Help Me Do This" to "Do This for Me"

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: Spoiler alert, but I know you're going to give us a demo of Toast IQ, and I think that's powerful, because ultimately it proves how people are interacting with your product. One thing I noticed, especially with AI, is that the user is changing their expectation from "tool, help me do this" to "tool, do this for me."

speaker: Maggie Crowley
text: I think about this a lot, because the dream, of course, is what you're saying: to actually hand off a workflow end to end. So many of us are trying out all these new consumer AI tools and playing around with them. Those tools and those patterns feel inevitable to me. But there's some unknown amount of time from when the consumer market has those things to when they're fully adopted in a B2B context, and it probably depends heavily on the type of user you have and the space you're in. So it's interesting to be in this moment where we see where things are going, we see where the behavior is going, and we have a chance to figure out how to do it well for our users. To me, it's the most interesting time to be building in a space like this. And I love building for a customer like ours, because they have such a low tolerance for doing AI for AI's sake. They don't care at all if it's AI or Toast IQ or whatever. All they care about is: did you help me with my business, and did you help me with a specific problem? So I'm really interested to see how it all plays out. The Clock on Consumer AI Patterns

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: You mentioned these new consumer AI agents. I've been obsessing over them. Literally yesterday I went to sleep at 3 a.m. because I couldn't stop; the thing kept doing things for me, and it was fun and addictive. It also made me miserable. But I can see how that B2C pattern that makes someone feel invincible could eventually apply to B2B and allow business owners of all kinds to have a much better understanding of their business, and eventually get to do things they used to do when the business was smaller.

speaker: Maggie Crowley
text: Absolutely. And there's almost a clock, because the second you start to see interactions like that in the consumer market, there's a certain amount of time until those patterns become standard. And then, if you have an AI product, your users expect that. So I also see it as: okay, we're seeing these patterns happen now, how long do I have before my users assume that's how my tool will work? I have that amount of time to make sure I can do whatever those things do. We have to stay relevant enough in the space. It's fun, because to me it means you almost have no idea where your product is going to go, and you have to figure out how to be more flexible, because you don't really know what the patterns are going to be, in terms of the interaction patterns, but also in terms of what the models can do. Before AI, building was almost getting boring, relatively. Now it's much more dynamic and interesting, because we have no idea what's coming.

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: You don't know where the limits are. Before, the constraints would define your behavior. Now you're like, "Hey, can you create this new button and do something else?"

speaker: Maggie Crowley
text: Totally. The Competitive Landscape

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: I also want to cover the market landscape. When you think about the restaurant, point of sale is important, and I imagine companies like Square are part of that market. But even more broadly, when I think about food delivery with companies like DoorDash or Uber Eats, or table reservations with OpenTable, or reputation management with Yelp, how are you thinking about your position in this bigger platform?

speaker: Maggie Crowley
text: It's a good question, and everybody is trying to figure out how the market is going to play out. I don't know that anybody knows how we're all going to interact and how it's all going to land. The way I think about this problem is: how do we make sure we're keeping our customers at the heart of what we're doing? It's so easy to get distracted by the competitive dynamics, the market dynamics, who's going to be the winner, whether there's going to be a winner, how it's all going to play out. It's interesting to game that out from a strategic standpoint. But at the end of the day, the company that wins, if there is such a thing, is the one that solves the right problem in the best way for their market and deeply understands it. So now, even more than before, the most important thing is to really understand the user and what they're up to. Be with them physically, go to their places, watch them do their work, be the person they can call. The more you do that, the better positioned you'll be for whatever the future holds. In the same way that three weeks ago we'd never heard of some of these consumer AI tools and now they're all we can talk about, who knows what new entrants will happen or what other companies will do? If you try to anchor too much on gaming that out, you're going to miss the point of right now, which is: build for your user and do everything you can for them, because that's what's going to make you successful no matter what happens in the market. Growth Levers as a Public Company

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: Looking at some of the market numbers: you had a killer quarter, a Q2 with one of the fastest, steepest growth curves in history, growing at $2.4 billion, 25% year over year, and profitable. At the same time, you also have to pick a lane. So from a strategic standpoint, how are you figuring out your growth levers?

speaker: Maggie Crowley
text: It's as simple as what I'm saying. The better we are at understanding what our customers need, the better able we are to build things they're willing to pay for. Especially in a business as tight as a restaurant, you don't have the option of just assuming people will pay for extra things. You have to understand the P&L of a restaurant to understand where any additional dollar you're going to charge is going to come from, and whether it's actually going to be worth their time. And especially being a public company, we have a really strong finance team who are amazing, and we've been really disciplined about that. So the way we think about building always has to be something that really matters for the user. That's how we think about growth: deeply understand what they need, solve real problems, and then the rest kind of figures itself out. From "We Manage Your POS" to "We Grow Your Restaurant"

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: One of the things I read about the positioning of your product, Toast IQ, is that you're going from "we manage your point of sale" to "we grow your restaurant." text: The marketing one is really interesting. That product has been so successful. A lot of the sweet spot for us is that a marketer or a restaurateur isn't necessarily someone who loves doing email marketing or online marketing or building a website. So they pay someone to do it, and that's really expensive, and it's a low-margin business. They're happy to pay less than they'd pay an agency to get a lot of what they're getting from the agency, but using AI. So that's been one of the breakthrough use cases for us. That team has done a really amazing job building an agent that solves a painful problem: driving demand for a restaurant.

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: So this is an agent that can do a lot of that marketing work on behalf of the restaurant, via email, text, and other channels.

speaker: Maggie Crowley
text: Yeah, it's called Toast IQ Grow, and the whole game of it is: how do we put butts in seats, and all the different pieces that go into that, helping our customers offload that work.

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia

speaker: Maggie Crowley
text: I feel like I'm a broken record here, but it's the same thing. The more we can spend our time really understanding the technology, the better we are at doing that for customers. So the way we structure our teams is we try to make sure we have a PM focused deeply in that kind of space, so they can figure out, with their technical counterparts, how to bring that solution to our users, rather than forcing a customer to figure it out themselves. We're doing that across basically every use case we can think of, trying to figure out what we can take off your plate with AI, what problems we can solve, and how we make it easy for you, so that as a customer you don't have to think about which model to use, which tool to use, whether to use Anthropic or OpenAI or an open weight model. We can do all that for them, so all they have to do is plug into Toast and it works. Why a VP Still Line-Manages a Frontline Team

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: As a VP of Product, you're not an IC anymore, but I imagine you're also carving out time to do some IC work, to stay in touch with customers. How does the day-to-day look now, different from before AI became that popular?

speaker: Maggie Crowley
text: I really think that in this day and age, if you don't keep a hand in how the teams are building, it's going to be really difficult to be a leader in nine months, a year, or two years, because the way teams build is so different. So whether that's finding a project to do on your own, or finding a way to be a line manager versus a manager of managers, at whatever level you're at, I think that's super critical for leaders right now. For me, the way I've done it is: any time a PM goes on parental leave, or we have an opening, I try to hop in and do that job for a little bit, to keep myself in the weeds on those products, and to make sure I understand what's going on at the frontline level. I also have areas where I don't have a middle-management layer and I manage the frontline team myself, because I want to stay close to the product. I think you can scale yourself as a leader much more effectively using AI tools, which lets you keep a flatter team than you used to. And if you don't do that as a leader, there's only so long until you don't understand how these tools work, and you're going to be somewhat irrelevant. Live Demo: Toast IQ

text: Totally. text: Yeah, we have partners we work with across basically the full lifecycle of a restaurant or retail shop.
